title: A design sweep is a map of a trade-off: read the axis range before the shape
summary: A one-parameter sweep (pressure drop against bore) and a two-parameter heatmap (required length against bore and wall superheat) are the two basic ways to size equipment. Both are only as informative as their axis ranges: a curve that looks steep can span a few percent, and a heatmap that looks complicated can depend on one variable.

media.alt: Line plot with markers of total fuel-coil pressure drop in pascals, about 3,270 to 3,520, on a logarithmic y axis against tube inner diameter from 5 to 15 mm. The curve dips to a minimum at 6 mm and then rises steadily, steepest at the largest diameters.

source.caption: Pressure-drop sweep vs tube diameter
source.note: Group explainer for the two sizing-analysis figures of the fuel vaporizer. The caption of the heatmap says 'heater zoning' but the axis is labelled wall-superheat design target K; the explainer follows the axis label.

read_the_figure.question: How do pressure drop and required heated length change as the tube bore and the wall-superheat target are varied, and where does the chosen design sit?
read_the_figure.axes: Figure 01: x is tube inner diameter D_i from 5 to 15 mm; y is total fuel-coil pressure drop in pascals on a logarithmic axis whose tick labels run from 3.3e3 to 3.5e3. Title: 50% ethanol, worst-case blend. Figure 02: x is the wall-superheat design target K from about 5 to 30 degrees C; y is D_i from 5 to 15 mm (uneven steps: 12.57 and 10.92 are catalogue sizes); colour is required single-zone length in metres, including a 15 percent margin, from below 20 to about 95 m.
look_at: Figure 01: the span of the y axis. Read the lowest and highest marker, about 3.27 and 3.52 kPa. The whole curve moves by 3.52 / 3.27 = 1.08, about 8 percent.
Figure 01: the minimum at 6 mm, then a steady rise; the 5 mm point is higher than 6 mm.
Figure 02: the columns. Colour changes strongly from left to right (K) and, for D_i of 8 mm and above, hardly at all from bottom to top: the cells in each column are the same shade.
Figure 02: the white star, labelled baseline (D = 6 mm, K = 15 K), L = 17.57 m, and the annotated grid minimum 6.12 m at D = 5 mm, K = 30 K, 'still 1.06x the 5.76 m built coil'.
read_the_figure.proves: Figure 01 shows that, for the worst-case blend, the pressure drop barely changes over the catalogue range, so it does not discriminate between bores. Figure 02 shows that the required length is set mainly by the wall-superheat target, and that even the most favourable grid corner needs a little more length than the coil that was built.
if_wrong: A curve plotted on a log axis over a narrow range looks like a linear plot with a large slope; reading it as 'large effect' is wrong.
A heatmap whose cells are uniform in one direction means the metric does not depend on that variable there, or that a limiter (a cap, a regime switch) has taken over. Both should be explained.
A baseline that is not at the optimum is fine if the other constraints are shown; if they are not, the reader cannot judge the choice.
must_check: The y-axis range and whether it starts at a meaningful value: for figure 01 it does not start at zero.
The conditions behind the sweep: blend, flow rate, outlet temperature (160 C is given in figure 02) and what is held fixed while D or K varies.
Whether the tube length is fixed or re-sized at each D in figure 01, since pressure drop depends on both.
Colour scale: figure 02 uses a sequential map, ordered correctly, with a colorbar and units.
A marker for the design actually chosen, and the constraints that exclude other cells.
as_drawn: Values below are read off the figures by eye. Figure 01: about 3.31 kPa at 5 mm, 3.27 at 6 mm, 3.30 at 7 mm, 3.35 at 9 mm, 3.39 at 12 mm and 3.52 at 15 mm.

Figure 02: the baseline length 17.57 m at K = 15 K scales as 1/K down the column: 17.57 x 15 / 5 = 52.7 m at K = 5 K, which matches the teal colour at D = 6 mm, K = 5 K (about 50 m). The annotated minimum 6.12 m divided by the built coil 5.76 m is 1.06, as stated.

The built coil (5.76 m) is much shorter than the single-zone baseline (17.57 m). The caption says 'single-zone', so the real design presumably uses more than one heating zone; the tube-sizing group shows a staged profile.

terms.meaning: The loss of static pressure along the coil from friction (and, if the fluid vaporises, acceleration). It sets the pump work.
The diameter of the flow passage.
The design temperature difference between the heated wall and the fluid it heats. A larger K means a larger driving temperature difference and a shorter tube.
The heated length needed to deliver the duty at the stated K, here with a 15 percent margin.
The ethanol-water mixture that makes the design hardest; here 50% ethanol (the longest-length blend in figure 02).
Dimensionless wall friction in a pipe.
The set of candidate designs described by the parameters that are free to change.

remember: Pressure drop at fixed flow in a long straight tube scales as one over D to the fifth power.
Required length at a given duty scales as one over the heat flux, which scales with the driving temperature difference.
Check the axis range: a few percent of variation can look dramatic on a zoomed axis.
A log axis on a narrow range hides the fact that the effect is small.
State what is held fixed in every sweep.

understand.title: Why length falls as K grows
understand.text: Heat delivered is flux times area. Flux scales with the temperature difference K between wall and fluid, so doubling K halves the area, and with it the length of a tube of fixed bore. The colour columns in figure 02 follow that law.

understand.title: Why figure 01 rises with bore
understand.text: In a straight pipe at fixed flow, a wider bore cuts the friction loss sharply. The plotted loss rises with bore, so the figure must contain something else: a length that changes with D, or a non-frictional term. The figure does not say which.

understand.title: What the baseline star tells you
understand.text: The star is the design choice at D = 6 mm and K = 15 K with 17.57 m. It sits in the middle of the colour range, not at the corner with the shortest length, so some other constraint (such as the wall ceiling shown in the tube-sizing group) is limiting K.

steps.title: Friction loss in a straight tube
steps.note: Darcy-Weisbach. L is the length, u the mean speed and rho the density.

steps.title: Express it with the mass flow
steps.note: Substituting the speed shows the D to the minus fifth dependence at fixed length and flow. A bore 20 percent larger cuts the loss to 1/1.2^5, about 40 percent.

steps.title: Energy balance for the length
steps.tex: \dot m\,\Delta h=q''\,\pi D\,L\quad\Rightarrow\quad L=\frac{\dot m\,\Delta h}{\pi D\,q''}
steps.note: The heat the fluid must receive equals the wall flux times the heated area.

steps.title: Flux from the superheat target
steps.note: With a film coefficient h the flux is h K. At fixed bore the length is inversely proportional to K, as the columns in figure 02 show: 17.57 m at 15 K becomes 52.7 m at 5 K (computed).

steps.title: Why a log axis hides small changes
steps.note: On a logarithmic axis equal ratios take equal distances. The whole curve spans 0.032 of a decade, about three percent of one decade, yet fills the plot because the axis was zoomed to it.

worked.title: Scale the baseline length to another superheat target
worked.problem: The baseline at D = 6 mm, K = 15 K needs 17.57 m (read from figure 02). Using L proportional to 1/K at fixed D, estimate the length at K = 30 K and compare with the grid minimum.

solution.text: Scale by the ratio of K values.
The grid minimum (5 mm, 30 K) is 6.12 m.

worked.answer: About 8.8 m at 6 mm and 30 K, 1.4 times the 6.12 m at 5 mm and 30 K: the smaller bore helps here, which the figure's bottom row also shows (darkest at 5 mm).

analyze.q: Figure 01 rises with bore although friction should fall as 1/D^5. List two things the sweep might include that explain this, and say which extra plot would separate them.
analyze.hint: Length re-sized at each D; acceleration pressure drop during vaporisation.

analyze.q: In figure 02, for D_i of 8 mm and above, each column is a single colour. What does that tell you about the model in that region?
analyze.hint: Is the metric independent of D, or capped?

analyze.q: The pressure drop varies by about 8 percent across the catalogue. Is the pressure drop a useful criterion for choosing the bore?
analyze.hint: Compare with the length variation in figure 02.

evaluate.q: The 6 mm point is the minimum of figure 01 and the baseline of figure 02. Is that coincidence supporting the choice, or does the weak variation make it meaningless?
evaluate.hint: A minimum of an 8 percent range is a weak argument.

evaluate.q: The caption says 'heater zoning' but the axis is wall-superheat K. How would you caption it so a reader is not misled?

create: Redraw figure 01 with a linear y axis from zero and the horizontal axis in the same catalogue sizes, and compare the visual impression.
Add to figure 02 a hatched region for designs that violate a stated constraint (for example the wall temperature ceiling), so the baseline's position is explained.

checks.q: Why does the required length fall as the wall-superheat target K rises?
checks.hint: Heat flux is proportional to K.
checks.answer: Flux grows with the driving temperature difference, so less heated area, hence less length, is needed for the same duty: L is proportional to 1/K.

checks.q: A 17.57 m baseline at K = 15 K: what length at K = 5 K?
Why can a log-axis plot of a range from 3.27 to 3.52 kPa be misleading?
checks.hint: How big is the real variation?
checks.answer: The axis is zoomed to that range, so an 8 percent change spans the plot. Reading it as a large effect would be wrong.

checks.q: Is the 6 mm bore supported by figure 01 alone?
checks.hint: Compare the size of the effect with plausible noise.
checks.answer: Not strongly: the curve changes by about 8 percent in total and 6 mm is only a shallow minimum; other criteria such as length, wall temperature and manufacturability must carry the decision.

checks.q: What extra layer would make figure 02 a decision map rather than a trend map?
checks.answer: Contours or hatching for constraint violations (wall ceiling, maximum length, pressure drop) and a marker for the feasible optimum.
